chief_complaint: chronic lower back pain improving with exercise, HLA-B27
hpi_details: A 29-year-old male presents to the clinic with chronic lower back pain that improves with exercise and is HLA-B27 positive. The pain has persisted for several months and has been gradually worsening, accompanied by generalized fatigue.
ideas: He thinks he herniated a spinal disc or pulled a deep lower back muscle from deadlifting at the gym.
concerns: He is worried that his spine will permanently stiffen and stop him from playing recreational soccer or staying active.
expectations: He hopes to get an MRI scan of his spine and a referral for physical therapy.

core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Ankylosing Spondylitis is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes NSAIDs, exercise and physical therapy, with rheumatology assessment for biologic therapy if disease remains active, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.

common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Ankylosing Spondylitis.
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Mechanical back pain without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Eye pain/redness.

boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective: Patient presenting with chief complaint of chronic lower back pain improving with exercise, HLA-B27. HPI: enthesitis, sacroiliitis.
reference_soap.objective: Focused physical exam and vital signs check. Tailored diagnostics for Ankylosing Spondylitis.
reference_soap.assessment: Condition highly suspicious for Ankylosing Spondylitis.
reference_soap.plan: Assess inflammatory-back-pain features, neurologic examination, uveitis, psoriasis, inflammatory bowel disease, infection risks, and mechanical alternatives; use pelvic radiography or MRI when clinically indicated. New urinary retention/incontinence, saddle anesthesia, progressive leg weakness, fever/systemic illness, or major trauma needs emergency evaluation for cauda equina syndrome, infection, fracture, or another urgent cause. NSAIDs require clinician review of renal, gastrointestinal, cardiovascular, pregnancy, and interaction risks. Rheumatology should direct biologic therapy after infection screening (including tuberculosis and hepatitis), vaccination review, and ongoing monitoring.

history.answer: My lower back has been aching for several months now, and it seems to be getting steadily worse.
It is down in my low back and across both buttocks, but it does not shoot down past my knees.
It started gradually around 6 to 8 months ago without any specific accident, fall, or heavy lifting.
It is a deep, constant, dull ache that sits around a 4 or 5 out of 10 on most days.
Sitting still or resting makes the stiffness worse, whereas getting up and moving around or doing light exercise actually helps relieve it. Coughing doesn't trigger sharp pain.
Yes, the pain frequently wakes me up in the second half of the night, and lying in bed doesn't help at all.
I wake up feeling very stiff every morning, and it usually takes more than an hour of walking around and stretching before it begins to loosen up.
No, I have not noticed any numbness, tingling sensations, or weakness in my legs or feet.
No, my bowel and bladder functions are completely normal, and I have no numbness around my groin or buttocks.
No, walking doesn't cause cramping or numbness in my legs; in fact, moving around actually eases the stiffness.
No fevers, chills, unexplained weight loss, or night sweats, although I have been feeling unusually tired and fatigued lately.
No, I have never had cancer or any tumors.
No, I haven't had any recent infections, food poisoning, spinal procedures, epidural injections, or intravenous drug use.
No, I have never been diagnosed with osteoporosis, never took long-term steroids, and have had no recent falls.
No, I have no pain or burning when I urinate, no blood in my urine, no stomach pain, and no throbbing sensation in my belly.
No, my eyes have not been red, painful, or unusually sensitive to light, and my vision has been completely normal.
Actually, both of my heels have been quite sore and tender, especially when I first step out of bed in the morning.
No chronic diarrhea, loose bowel movements, stomach cramps, or blood in my stools.
No, I haven't had any scaly skin patches, scalp rash, or pitted fingernails.
I tried over-the-counter ibuprofen a few times, and it noticeably eased both the stiffness and the aching, though I haven't taken it on a regular schedule.
I work as a software engineer sitting at a desk all day, which really stiffens my back up. The chronic ache has been frustrating, but my mood is otherwise stable.
I figured I must have slipped a disc or strained a deep back muscle while lifting weights at the gym.
I'm really worried that my spine is freezing up and I won't ever be able to play soccer or work out again.
I'm hoping to get an MRI to see which nerve is pinched and a referral to physical therapy.
I have always been generally healthy and have no history of chronic medical illnesses.
I have never had any surgeries and have never been hospitalized.
I am not taking any daily prescription medications, over-the-counter drugs, or herbal supplements.
I have no known allergies to any medications, foods, or materials.
I have never smoked cigarettes or used any tobacco products.
I only drink alcohol socially, perhaps one or two beers on the weekend, and nothing during the work week.
My uncle on my father's side had chronic back stiffness and spine trouble, but neither of my parents has an autoimmune disease.

exam.finding: Alert, well-nourished young male, shifting position periodically while seated to relieve back discomfort.
Blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, pulse 72 beats/min, respiratory rate 14 breaths/min, body temperature 36.7 °C, oxygen saturation 99% on room air.
Conjunctivae clear and sclerae anicteric without erythema, ciliary flush, or photophobia; pupils round and reactive to light.
Soft, non-tender to palpation throughout; no palpable pulsatile abdominal aortic mass or organomegaly.
No costovertebral angle tenderness on percussion on either side.

Tenderness elicited over bilateral sacroiliac joints and lower lumbar spinous processes; reduced lumbar spine flexion on modified Schober test (12.5 cm); straight-leg raise test is negative bilaterally up to 80 degrees.
Focal tenderness over bilateral Achilles tendon insertions without swelling; no peripheral joint effusions, warmth, or synovitis in knees, ankles, or wrists.
Motor strength 5/5 bilaterally across all lower extremity muscle groups, including hip flexors, knee extensors, and ankle dorsiflexors/plantarflexors.
Intact light touch and pinprick sensation throughout bilateral lower extremity dermatomes (L2 to S1) and intact perineal sensation.
Symmetric 2+ patellar and Achilles deep tendon reflexes bilaterally; bilateral plantar responses are flexor (negative Babinski).
No erythematous scaly plaques, extensor surface lesions, dactylitis, or nail dystrophy/pitting seen.
